html: Star Trek and the perfection of giving

speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
html: Timothy Lowenhaupt: Next slide. This is when my nerdery comes out. This is the Starship Enterprise, Brian — the Next Generation. The series I grew up with, the moral backbone of my childhood. And there's something interesting that happens in this world.

So Shantideva says to us — and this is how Star Trek relates to Shantideva — Shantideva says, does the perfection of giving depend upon the external perfection? Like, by giving things away, say to people in need, people in poverty, hungry people — if you reach the perfection of giving, does that mean that all of those things go away? Does that mean that poverty goes away, that hunger goes away, that illness goes away? Or does it mean, you haven't reached the perfection until that happens — and somehow there's something wrong with your perfection of giving because people are still hungry? That's the question he's asking.

So why do I have a picture of the Starship Enterprise? Because in this world — and this is the imaginary that I grew up with when I was a kid — so when we're doing these meditations from Geshe Michael's new meditations from Malaysia, and the subsequent ones, and we're thinking about the books and the songs and the television shows and the things that appeared in our world, and we pull and we try to logically figure out, if this was here for me, what seeds did I plant in the previous life to create this? This is what I grew up with. This universe is 300 years in the future, and they've achieved a certain kind of perfection.

I have a couple of quotes that I happen to just know, because I'm a nerd. One of them is that there's an episode where they meet somebody from our time period, from the 20th century. And the captain says, a lot has changed in 300 years. And he says, people are no longer obsessed with the accumulation of things. We've eliminated hunger, want, and the need for possessions. It's a pretty cool world to think about — a place where they don't want things in the same way. They don't need to have stuff, like how much stuff we need. We don't need a shopping mall full of butt masks. Actually, it is that way. They don't have hunger anymore. They've created all the technology that — if you need it, it's just available.

And so the question is, did humanity perfect giving? That's my question. Did they perfect giving because they eliminated hunger? And this is what Shantideva asks: what's a perfection, and what's the result of the perfection? Is the result of the perfection something external, like there's no hunger left? And we have to think of it this way: if removing all hunger was the essence of the perfection of giving — or removing all poverty — then the enlightened beings of the past would not have perfected giving. I'll say it again: if removing the poverty of the world is the essence of the perfection of giving, then the enlightened beings of the past would not have perfected giving. Why? Because we see poverty around us all the time.

And so the perfection of giving is defined in a really cool way: it is the perfection of willingness to give. It is the willingness to give the things that you have. And that's always, always explained within one's current ability. I could empty my bank account right now and just give all the money away — but then I wouldn't be able to pay my bills, I wouldn't be able to eat. The willingness to give doesn't mean you give away everything. You give it away within your current ability to give. And so there are certain kinds of rules about giving.
Giving within your means and caring for the body

speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
html: Timothy Lowenhaupt: So, slide 30, Brian. For example, when you partake of food, ideally you should give equal parts to everybody. Not take a big bowl and be like, here's my plate of food, and, well, you only get one bite, you're smaller than me, it's okay, you only need that, I need all of this. There is a difference. I was watching this guy this morning at breakfast — I get these little tiny bowls of congee, and he was just — I'm like, dude, what are you eating? The guy's huge, it's like 200 centimeters, and I don't know how many kilograms, but probably 100, 110 kilograms. The guy was big. And he's just shoveling the food in. That's not what it means. It's like giving equal share to people. When you have food with everybody, make sure everybody has some and has enough. And a lot of times you do it in your own mind — I got offered a plate of food, there's no one else around me, but I can have in my mind that I should offer an equal share to all the different kinds of beings: all the animals, all the spirits, all the people who are sick, all the people who have no one to protect them. And you should only eat what you need to eat. Don't take more than what you need — and our culture is, not so much here in Taiwan, but in the United States, people are incredibly unhealthy and they eat way more than they ever possibly need to survive. It's an obsession, and it's a hoarding — mine, mine, mine. And you can see it in the culture, you can see it in the politics. Mine. Keep it from me. Don't share.

And so the idea is that Shantideva says a bodhisattva — so there's the monk level, and then there's a bodhisattva level. The bodhisattva should even go to the place of giving away the possessions they have — give away everything except for their robes. They need the robes still. You should be able to give everything away, when you're ready to. And that's the rule — when you're ready to, and we'll talk about it in a second.

Next slide. You should also, at the same time, protect your body, and not do things to your body that could hurt it. Like skydiving. Sure, skydiving's fun, it's exhilarating — look, these guys are having a good time. I looked at this picture and I was like, I really hope the parachute opens. I was trying to imagine myself doing this — packing my own parachute — and is it going to work? And then worrying about it. One of my friends broke his leg landing — shattered his leg, couldn't walk again, well, walked, but kind of walked with a limp. You don't need to do things that risk your body. Why? Because this body is the only thing that can become enlightened. This body is the vessel that can become enlightened. If you risk that body for minor goals, like skydiving, or doing things to it for a short-term benefit — like some people, I was trying to think of an example earlier today, people who inject themselves with hormones like testosterone to get overly bigger muscles. For what purpose? It hurts your body in the long run, it makes you sick in the long run. The thing to do is to care for it — to see this as a holy vessel.

I've told you all the story about when I was in Malaysia and I got on a scooter. The first thing that happened is I ran off the road and fell and landed on my head and scraped my whole side. And the first thing I thought was, this is why Geshe Michael told me not to get on a scooter — because it's dangerous. You've got to think that way. Like, what kind of car do you buy? Do you wear your seatbelt? What's the chance of getting in a car accident where you're going to need this seatbelt? Very small. But if you get in that accident and you don't have the seatbelt on, it's going to hurt, or you'll die. So Shantideva is saying, look, you've got to take care of this. Don't do unnecessary harm to it. First of all, eat what you need — don't overeat, because overeating causes problems. Share. Secondly, take care of this body. It's going to get old — if you're lucky, it gets old, meaning if you live long enough.
When to give your body — and the gift of presence

speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
html: Timothy Lowenhaupt: And then thirdly — this is what I wanted to talk about before we end — when we're talking about giving, and this idea of the perfection of giving, the willingness to give: when is the proper time to do it, and to give one's own body? Because you've heard the stories of the bodhisattvas, like, oh, you need an eye? Here's my eye — and I give you my eye and then you can see again. Most of us probably aren't willing to give an eye. And even if we had a moment of, I'm going to give my eye, you would probably have regret afterward — not only the pain, but then you can't see. So you have to be in a very, very high place to be able to give your body to the point where you would really be able to perfect giving on that level. So don't take those stories literally. You're not a bad bodhisattva if you don't give your eyeball, or cut off part of your body.

I use the example of a kidney, because Geshe Michael is looking for a kidney transplant. A healthy person can give one of their kidneys and be fine. But even then, I've thought about it, and I'm like, yeah, I can give that to my teacher — and then I'm like, can I? How would I feel about that? Besides — even if I were a candidate — the whole process of the surgery and the recovery, and then knowing that this could affect me later in life: if I get my own kidney disease, now I only have one kidney. There are all these possibilities. And so the idea is that if you would regret it, you're not ready for it.

There's a story of Khen Rinpoche — one of his students was so devoted after a really big teaching and said, I want to give you a house. Let me give you my house, you need a much nicer house. And he said, no. And Geshe Michael's like, Rinpoche, we could really use that. We could really use this. And he said, no — she's going to regret giving that away. And so that's where you have to work with what's within your means. But it doesn't mean that you're reducing the power of your giving by giving within your means.

So there are all these stories about bodhisattvas that do all these great things, these extraordinary acts of giving. And Shantideva is saying — just plain old kindness. Just simple giving. Giving your presence — not gifts, but giving your presence, being present with people. Listening. Your time, your energy, your care, your love. All of those things are giving. And as you get better at it and stronger with it, then you become less attached to your things, and you know how you got the things in the first place, so then it becomes easier to give extra things. It becomes easier to say, here, have my jacket, have this extra shirt, I have this extra money — a bank account that's just there for other people's emergencies. But there are times when I'm like, wow, I really could use that money because I'm kind of having an emergency too. And then I have to check in with my motivation: no, that was guided toward other people. But in a pinch, would I take the money for myself? Would I let myself starve because I said that money was for somebody else? Then you're violating the other rules of care. But I'm doing fine financially. And why am I doing fine financially? Because I have this other account that I give money to, that I put money in every month. And then when someone has an issue, I'm like, oh, look at this — here's a thousand dollars. And they're like, what? And I'm like, yeah. And it's so joyful.

So if you're having money issues, take 5%, 3% — make a special bank account, or piggy bank, or whatever. And just collect that money for other people, within your means. Some people make a lot of money, they can do 10%; but maybe only 1% for you at this point. It doesn't matter. It's not about who's a better Dharma practitioner. Because, again, how we started the class: you're not better because you save 10% and I only save 1%. The person with 1% has an equal chance of becoming enlightened as the person who's saving 10%. You have to understand why.
Closing: finishing the courses strong

speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
html: Timothy Lowenhaupt: So we didn't cover every little piece of that class — we only missed one section: how the six perfections relate to each other. And you can do that in your study groups. Oh my gosh, that was an epic class.

It's good to see all of you again. We're now two-thirds of the way through. ACI 16 is done. ACI 17 is now done. We have one course left, everybody. Let's finish strong. This series, for those who don't know, is called Kompletion Karma. Let's finish the 18 courses. There's a power in doing this together. There's power in getting through all of the prescribed courses from Geshe Michael. But what it'll do to your mind to actually finish it — just you wait. It's going to be pretty cool. I know a lot of the group here, we're only halfway through — don't worry, we'll get them done. But those of you online, we only have one left — keep going. We only have September, October, November, December, January. We have five more months left. We can do this.

And today we have — excuse me, we have a transmission in a month and a half. Good job. Look at the completion karma you created. You didn't have to finish the 18 courses to get a transmission. Everyone thinks you've got to do your 18 courses to get Diamond Way — you don't have to finish it to get Diamond Way. Good job. Way to change the karma of that. But that doesn't mean that we shouldn't finish.

I'm very, very proud of all of you who are doing this. I'm very proud of the study group leaders. I've been watching the scheduling — I'm not actually going to the study groups — and it's an amazing thing what you're all doing. And what we're going to be doing after transmission — you have no clue what's coming. With this number of people committed and shifting their seeds in this way, you have no idea what's coming. There's so much good coming. It's extraordinary. So I'm happy all of you are here. Thank you for joining. Tonight's my last night in Taiwan — I'm leaving tomorrow morning. So thank you all for hosting me here, letting me teach here while we're on this cool journey together. So thank you once again. And on your way out, please turn on your microphones and say goodbye.

speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
html: Timothy Lowenhaupt: Thank you so much. Bye-bye. Bye, everyone.
